'''''Lavandula stoechas''''', the '''Spanish lavender''' or '''topped lavender''' (U.S.) or '''French lavender''' (U.K.),<ref name = RHSAZ/> is a [[species]] of [[Lavandula|lavender]] native to the [[Mediterranean Basin]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Lavandula stoechas L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:449089-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=29 July 2024 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Seidel |first=Dankwart |year=2002 |title=Flowers on the Mediterranean |location=Munich, Germany |publisher=BLV |ISBN=3-405-16294-7}}</ref>{{page needed |date=May 2024}}

== Taxonomy ==
The flower was first recorded by Greek botanist [[Pedanius Dioscorides]] as the name {{lang|el|στοιχάς}} ''stoikhas''<ref name="GEL">{{cite dictionary |url=https://www.perseus.tufts.edu/hopper/text?doc=Perseus%3Atext%3A1999.04.0057%3Aalphabetic+letter%3D*s111%3Aentry+group%3D80%3Aentry%3Dstoixa%2Fs |title=στοιχάς |dictionary=A Greek-English Lexicon |last1=Liddell |first1=Henry George |last2=Scott |first2=Robert |publisher=Perseus Digital Library |date= 1940 }}</ref> coming from  [[Îles d'Hyères|the Stoechades Islands]], the Greek name became its [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]].<ref name="Lis">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8gmsF-FQWuUC |editor-last=Lis-Balchin |editor-first=Maria |year=2002 |title=Lavender: The genus ''Lavandula'' |location= London, England, UK |publisher=Taylor and Francis |page=17 |isbn=0-415-28486-4 }}</ref><ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>{{page needed |date=May 2024}}

=== Subspecies ===
The recognised subspecies are: 

*''L. stoechas ssp. luisieri'', native to the southwest quadrant of the [[Iberian Peninsula]] (southern Portugal and southwest Spain). It has  lanceolate axilary leaves that are much larger than those of the nominal subspecies, along with a greyish [[indumentum]] (opposing the whitish indumentum of the nominal subspecies).<ref>{{cite web |title=Lavandula |url=http://www.floraiberica.es/floraiberica/texto/pdfs/12_140_37_Lavandula.pdf#page=7 |publisher=[[Flora Iberica]] |access-date=29 July 2024}}</ref>

== Description ==
It is an evergreen shrub that usually grows to between {{convert|30-100|cm}} tall, but occasionally up to {{convert|2|m|ft}} tall in the subspecies ''L. stoechas'' subsp. ''luisieri''. Its [[leaf|leaves]] are 1–4 cm long, greyish and [[tomentose]]. The [[inflorescence]] is crowned by a mass of purple elongated ovoid bracts about 5 cm long. Lower flowers form a tight rectangle in cross-section. The upper of the five teeth has a wrong-heart-shaped appendage. The crown is blackish-violet, up to 8 mm long and indistinct two-lipped.

The [[flower]]s, which appear in late spring and early summer, are pink to purple, produced on spikes 2 cm long at the top of slender, leafless stems {{convert|10|-|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} long; each flower is subtended by a [[bract]] 4–8 mm long. At the top of the spike are a number of much larger, sterile bracts (no flowers between them), 10–50 mm long and bright [[lavender (color)|lavender]] [[purple]] (rarely white). It blooms in spring and early summer, from the month of March in its native habitat, depending on the climate in which it grows.<ref name="Upson and Andrews">Upson and Andrews; The Genus Lavandula</ref>

== Cultivation ==
This species is more tender than common lavender (''[[Lavandula angustifolia]]''), being less frost-resistant, but harsher and more resinous in its oils. Like other lavenders, it is associated with hot, dry, sunny conditions in [[alkali soils|alkaline soils]].  However, it tolerates a range of situations, though it may be short-lived. [[Hardy (plants)|Hardy]] down to {{convert|-10 |C|F|abbr=on}}<ref name = RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref> ([[USDA]] zones 8–10).

The following [[cultivar]]s have won the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]]:-<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 59 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 19 March 2018}}</ref>
*'Ballerina'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/197137/Lavandula-Ballerina/Details | title = ''Lavandula'' 'Ballerina' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 19 March 2020}}</ref> 
*'Pretty Polly' <ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/227001/Lavandula-Pretty-Polly/Details | title = ''Lavandula'' 'Pretty Polly' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 1 October 2020}}</ref> 
*'Willow Vale'<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Lavandula'' 'Willow Vale' |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/175774/Lavandula-Willow-Vale/Details | access-date=23 February 2020}}</ref>

==Other uses==
The flowers are used in [[aromatherapy]] to prepare infusions and essential oils that contain [[ketone]]s (d-[[camphor]] and d-[[fenchone]]) and alcohols ([[borneol]] and [[terpineol]]).<ref>{{cite book|last=Bown|first=Deni|title=The Royal Horticultural Society Encyclopedia of Herbs and Their Uses|year=2002|edition=Revised|publisher=DK|isbn=1-4053-0059-0|pages=257}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
Since its introduction into Australia, it has become an [[invasive species]], widely distributed within the continent. It has been declared a noxious weed in Victoria since 1920. It also is regarded as a weed in parts of Spain.<ref>Csurches S., Edwards R.; National Weeds Program, Potential Environmental Weeds in Australia, Candidate Species for Preventative Control; Queensland Department of Natural Resources. January 1998 {{ISBN|0-642-21409-3}}</ref>
